New Signature is a PVP wormhole alliance living in a C5-C2 looking to acquire more PVP pilots. We are a mature group of players with jobs and families (average age ~35) who understand that the real world trumps EVE concerns every single time. We are looking for like-minded pilots who are interested in jumping on, shooting the shit, and trying to shoot other peoples' shit while we're at it. While there are obviously many isk-making opportunities in a C5, we mainly use them for SRP and to fund ships for pew. We're not interested in acquiring the risk-averse or those whose main concern is isk.

 

What we offer:

  • -Tight knit group of mature and friendly players

  • -SRP program for fleet ops

  • -Capital escalations and access to C2 sites for solo running

  • -Alliance Siggy and TeamSpeak server

  • -Infinite supply of puns and dad jokes

  • -Alliance scapegoat to place all blame onto

  • -Ability to fly any of the T2 scan frigates and knowledge of scanning

  • -Teamspeak 3 + mic, and be on comms whenever active in the wormhole

  • -Full API key

  • -Willingness to follow the few alliance rules that we do have

 

Things we like to see:

  • -Familiarity with d-scan and combat probing

  • -Some wormhole experience

Would this be a good way to implement computer physics engines because you could avoid more expensive computations?

Well according to this presentation by the author, I'm pretty sure it does...

But most computer programs have transcendental trigonometry built in. So I think you would have to build the program from the ground up to be able to use this type of geometry.

The reason I think it's faster is that it refuses to use infinite numbers and their functions (eg: sine, cosine..) and instead using quadratic forms...

Therefore, you end up with a number instead of a function! Just that fact should make computations faster...

I would love a computer programmer to back me up though, I've only ordered the book (I don't like youtube channels to learn but his channel seems pretty interesting!

Edit : here you can find more of his research. It seems to be more "pure math" than physics though, although there is a paper on quark/gluon theory, which if you've followed the penta-quark CERN discovery is pretty exciting!

Wow, that was very dense.

So chips have hardware multipliers but usually trig functions and roots are not on the CPU. The key advantage would be if you could get all your computations done with addition (super fast) and multiplication (quick) and completely avoid expensive operations like inverse square root. He doesn't actually totally avoid non rational numbers but he seems to be sticking with constructable numbers which could be represented exactly in the computer fairly cheaply. Also for computational physics particularly graphics what you want is a system you can cheaply approximate. I'd have to do quite a bit of work to see if there are really good shortcuts available from this.
